## The project endpoint
The Foundry SDK (`azure-ai-projects`) is a thin client over all Foundry project APIs, reached through **one project endpoint**:
`https://<resource-name>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project-name>`
The Python client README says you find it on the Foundry project home page. With a custom subdomain, the subdomain replaces the resource name.
## Two client types from one endpoint
- **Project client** (`AIProjectClient`): Foundry-native operations, for example listing connections, reading project properties, enabling tracing.
- **OpenAI-compatible client** (`project.get_openai_client()`): Responses, agents, evaluations, fine-tuning.
## Troubleshooting 404s
Learn's SDK troubleshooting section: for "Connection refused or 404 Not Found", verify the resource and project names and check that the URL has the `services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project-name>` format. The `openai.azure.com/openai/v1` address is the OpenAI SDK endpoint of the resource; it has no project APIs such as connections.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Resource Manager scope:** management.azure.com is the control plane for creating and configuring resources; AIProjectClient calls the Foundry data plane.
- ✗ **B. v1 route plus project:** there's no project segment under /openai/v1; that route serves OpenAI-style inference for the resource, not project operations.
- ✗ **C. Deployment URL:** that's an older per-deployment inference address; it reaches one model, not the project's connections, datasets or evaluations.
- ✓ **D. Project endpoint (correct):** AIProjectClient expects the `services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project>` URL, which is the only address that exposes project operations such as listing connections.

## Key idea
AIProjectClient takes the project endpoint `https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project>`; the /openai/v1 address belongs to the OpenAI SDK.
Q007203:
## Foundry roles (renamed)
Foundry's built-in roles were recently renamed; role IDs and permissions didn't change:
- **Foundry User** (formerly Azure AI User)
- **Foundry Project Manager** (formerly Azure AI Project Manager)
- **Foundry Account Owner** (formerly Azure AI Account Owner)
- **Foundry Owner** (formerly Azure AI Owner)
## Which role for which task
Learn's SDK overview lists roles "at the narrowest scope":
- **Foundry User on the Foundry project** for day-to-day development.
- **Foundry Project Manager on the project** to manage an existing project and its connections.
- **Foundry Account Owner on the Foundry resource** to create projects or manage account-level resources; a resource-group assignment only when creating a Foundry resource, activated just in time through Privileged Identity Management.
The cloud evaluation and portal evaluation articles also list the Foundry User role on the project as the prerequisite for running evaluations.
## If the token request fails
The SDK troubleshooting tips: run `az login`, then confirm at least Foundry User on the project.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Foundry User on the project (correct):** it covers building and testing with models and evaluations in that project and nothing more, which is the narrowest fit for a developer's daily work.
- ✗ **B. Project Manager:** managing the project and its connections is an administrative task; running evaluations only needs Foundry User.
- ✗ **C. Permanent resource-group Owner:** Learn recommends just-in-time elevation only when creating a Foundry resource, and Owner grants control over every resource in the group.
- ✗ **D. Account Owner on the resource:** that role is for creating projects and managing account-level resources, far more than calling models needs.

## Key idea
Give developers Foundry User on the Foundry project; reserve Project Manager and Account Owner for managing projects and resources.
Q007204:
## State in the Responses API
Learn describes the Responses API as producing **stateful, multi-turn responses**. Responses are stored by the service (by default for 30 days), so a later request can refer to an earlier one.
## Two ways to carry context
- **`previous_response_id` chaining**: "Chain turns by passing the previous response ID to `previous_response_id`." Each later request sends only the new user input; the service supplies the earlier turns.
- **Manual chaining**: the app keeps a list of input items, appends `response.output` and the next user message, and sends the whole list each time.
## Example
`first = client.responses.create(model="support-chat", input="My router keeps rebooting.")`
`second = client.responses.create(model="support-chat", previous_response_id=first.id, input="It started after the firmware update.")`
Learn's compaction section repeats the rule for this pattern: with `previous_response_id`, "pass only the new user message on each turn and carry the latest response ID forward."

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Transcript and id together:** this duplicates history the service already has, raising token use without improving recall, which is the opposite of the goal.
- ✗ **B. Transcript in a connection:** connections store how a project authenticates to other resources; the Responses API doesn't read conversation history from them.
- ✗ **C. Bigger first output:** output token limits cap how much the model writes; they don't create memory for later requests.
- ✓ **D. New message plus previous_response_id (correct):** the service already holds the earlier response, so linking to its id preserves context while each request carries only the new turn.

## Key idea
With the Responses API, continue a conversation by sending only the new input and `previous_response_id` set to the last response's id.
Q007205:
## Manual chaining
Learn shows two ways to chain Responses API turns. Besides `previous_response_id`, you can "manually carry forward output items in the next request":
`inputs = [{"type": "message", "role": "user", "content": "..."}]`
`response = client.responses.create(model=deployment, input=inputs)`
`inputs += response.output`
`inputs.append({"role": "user", "type": "message", "content": "next question"})`
`second = client.responses.create(model=deployment, input=inputs)`
## Why choose it
- The app owns the full history, so it can trim, redact or persist it in its own store.
- Later turns don't rely on the service's stored response objects.
- Learn's compaction guidance calls this **stateless input-array chaining**, the alternative to `previous_response_id` chaining.
## What a model doesn't do
The model itself has no memory between calls. Anything it should know about earlier turns must be in the request or linked through a stored response.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Model memory:** models are stateless between requests; without history in the input or a linked response, the next turn starts from nothing.
- ✗ **B. Output text in instructions:** instructions carry developer guidance; copying just the final text loses the earlier user turns and any tool call items in the output.
- ✓ **C. Append output items and the new message (correct):** the app sends the full item history each time, so the model has the earlier turns without relying on stored responses.
- ✗ **D. previous_response_id with empty input:** this is the service-side chaining the architects want to avoid, and a turn still needs the new user message.

## Key idea
For app-managed state, append `response.output` and the next user message to the input list and send the list every turn.
Q007206:
## Long-running reasoning tasks
Reasoning models such as o3 can think for a long time on complex tasks. Holding an HTTP request open for minutes is fragile: proxies, load balancers and browsers time out.
## Background mode
Learn: "Background mode lets you run long-running tasks asynchronously with reasoning models such as o3 and o1-pro. ... When a request is sent with `"background": true`, the task is processed asynchronously, and you poll for its status."
- The call returns immediately with a **response id** and a `queued` status.
- The app polls with `client.responses.retrieve(id)` while the status is `queued` or `in_progress`.
- At a terminal status (for example `completed`), the output is available. The id can also be used to stream or cancel.
## Example pattern
The web tier starts the task, saves the id with the user's job, and the page checks the job status every few seconds. Learn notes a known performance issue when combining background mode with streaming.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Chat Completions streaming:** streaming keeps one connection open for the whole task, which is the fragile part; background mode exists on the Responses API for exactly this case.
- ✓ **B. Background mode and polling (correct):** the request returns at once with an id, so no HTTP call has to stay open while the model reasons, and the app collects the result when the status is final.
- ✗ **C. Bigger output limit:** `max_output_tokens` caps generated tokens (including reasoning tokens); it doesn't return partial work early, and a higher cap only lets the task run longer.
- ✗ **D. Many tiny requests:** splitting a coherent analysis loses context between pieces, and there's no one-minute limit that forces it.

## Key idea
For multi-minute reasoning tasks, send Responses requests with `background=True` and poll the response id until it reaches a final status.
Q007207:
## Vision-enabled chat models
Learn describes vision-enabled chat models as large multimodal models that "can analyze images and provide textual responses to questions about them". The current list includes the o-series reasoning models, the GPT-5 series, the GPT-4.1 series and the GPT-4o series. You use them by calling the Chat Completions API on a supported deployment.
## Shape of a multimodal message
Instead of a plain string, the user message's `content` becomes an **array of parts**:
`{"role": "user", "content": [`
`  {"type": "text", "text": "What part is cracked?"},`
`  {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "<image url>"}}`
`]}`
The question and the image arrive in the same turn, so the model can reason over both together. The URL must be reachable by the service (Learn's samples use a publicly accessible image URL).
## Why not preprocess
OCR only extracts text and would miss the visual crack. Captioning first loses detail the question needs. A multimodal model answers directly from the pixels.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Text part plus image_url part (correct):** a vision-enabled deployment such as gpt-4.1 reads both parts of the same user message and answers the question about the image.
- ✗ **B. OCR first:** vision-enabled models accept image parts directly, and OCR would discard the visual damage the technician is asking about.
- ✗ **C. Separate image deployment:** one deployment of a vision-enabled model handles text and images together; a caption-then-answer chain adds latency and loses detail.
- ✗ **D. URL as text in the system message:** a URL written as plain text is just characters; the model only treats an image as input when it arrives as an image content part.

## Key idea
To ask about an image, send a user message whose content array has a text part and an `image_url` part to a vision-enabled deployment.
Q007208:
## Different model families, different endpoints
Learn's SDK overview lists which SDK and endpoint to use:
- **OpenAI SDK**: `https://<resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1`, for Azure OpenAI models and models sold by Azure through Responses or Chat Completions.
- **Foundry SDK**: the project endpoint, for agents, evaluations and project features.
- **Anthropic SDK**: `https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/anthropic`, for Anthropic Claude models deployed in Foundry.
## Claude in Foundry
"Claude models use a separate `/anthropic` endpoint and the Anthropic Messages API, not the OpenAI-compatible endpoint." The Messages API is at `.../anthropic/v1/messages`.
## Example
`client = AnthropicFoundry(azure_ad_token_provider=token_provider, base_url="https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/anthropic")`
`client.messages.create(model="<claude-deployment>", messages=[...], max_tokens=1024)`
Keyless auth works the same way as for other models: a bearer token provider for the `https://ai.azure.com/.default` scope. The `model` value is still the deployment name.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Anthropic SDK on /anthropic (correct):** Claude deployments in Foundry are served by the Anthropic Messages API on the resource's /anthropic endpoint, so the OpenAI-compatible route can't handle them.
- ✗ **B. Separate workspace:** the scenario's Claude deployment already lives in the Foundry resource; it only needs the right endpoint and SDK.
- ✗ **C. Project client and connection:** the project endpoint serves Foundry features over the Responses API; Learn sends Claude traffic to /anthropic and doesn't require an Anthropic connection.
- ✗ **D. Chat Completions on v1:** Learn says Claude uses the separate /anthropic endpoint, not the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so switching OpenAI methods doesn't help.

## Key idea
Call Claude deployments in Foundry with the Anthropic SDK at `https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/anthropic`, not the OpenAI v1 endpoint.
Q007209:
## How tool_choice works
When a request defines function tools, `tool_choice` decides whether the model may, must or must not call them. Learn's function calling article describes three settings:
- `"auto"` (the default): "the model decides on its own if it should call a function and if so which function to call". A plain-text answer is allowed.
- A **named tool object** forces one function: `tool_choice={"type": "function", "function": {"name": "record_ticket"}}`.
- `"none"` forces a user-facing message, so no function is called.
## Parallel calls are a different setting
`parallel_tool_calls` controls whether one response may hold several tool calls. Setting it to false limits the model to one call per turn; it doesn't make a call mandatory.
## Example
A triage pipeline that always needs structured category and priority values names record_ticket in `tool_choice`, reads `tool_calls[0].function.arguments`, and can add `strict: true` to the function so the arguments follow its schema.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. auto with a better description:** auto still lets the model choose a text reply; a clearer description may reduce misses but can't guarantee a call.
- ✗ **B. parallel_tool_calls false:** it caps how many calls one response may contain; under the default auto choice the model can still answer in text.
- ✗ **C. none:** this setting forces a user-facing message and prevents any function call, which is the opposite of what triage needs.
- ✓ **D. Named tool object (correct):** naming record_ticket in `tool_choice` makes the call mandatory, so every ticket returns arguments the pipeline can parse instead of free text.

## Key idea
To make the model always call one specific function, set `tool_choice` to a named tool object; "auto" lets it choose and "none" blocks calls.
Q007210:
## Structured outputs for function calling
Function calling lets the model return a tool call with JSON arguments that your code executes. Setting `strict: true` on a function definition applies **structured outputs** to those arguments, so they follow the tool's JSON Schema.
## The parallel calls limitation
Models that support parallel function calling can return several tool calls in one response (for example, one per booking). Learn's structured outputs article states: "Structured outputs are not supported with parallel function calls. When using structured outputs set `parallel_tool_calls` to false."
With `parallel_tool_calls=false`, the model requests one call per turn: the app runs book_flight, returns the result, and the model then requests book_hotel, each with schema-conformant arguments.
## Related controls
- `tool_choice: "auto"` (default): the model decides whether and which tool to call.
- `tool_choice` set to a named function forces that function; `"none"` forces a user-facing message.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. More completion tokens:** the arguments are malformed because of parallel calls, not truncation, so a bigger limit doesn't fix the schema mismatch.
- ✗ **B. Remove strict:** dropping strict removes schema enforcement entirely; strict mode works with multiple tools as long as calls aren't parallel.
- ✓ **C. parallel_tool_calls false (correct):** Learn documents that strict structured outputs don't apply to parallel calls, so turning parallel calls off restores schema-conformant arguments for each booking.
- ✗ **D. tool_choice none:** this stops tool calls altogether and forces the app to parse free text, giving up the structured arguments the design relies on.

## Key idea
When function tools use `strict: true` structured outputs, set `parallel_tool_calls` to false.
Q007211:
## Who runs a function tool
With function calling, the model never executes code. Learn: "The model generates function calls and structured arguments based on the functions you specify. Your application executes the functions and returns the results to the model, so you remain in control of the actions taken."
## The Responses API loop
1. Send the request with `tools=[{"type": "function", "name": "get_order_status", "parameters": {...}}]`.
2. Read `response.output`. For each item with `type == "function_call"`, parse `item.arguments` (a JSON string) and run your function.
3. Send a new request with `previous_response_id=response.id` and `input` containing `{"type": "function_call_output", "call_id": item.call_id, "output": json.dumps(result)}`.
4. Read `final.output_text`.
## Why call_id matters
When a response contains several calls, each result must reference the `call_id` of the call it answers so the model can match them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Name as user message:** the model can't execute app code; resending the name just restarts the request without any order data.
- ✓ **B. Execute and return function_call_output (correct):** the app runs the function and returns the result tied to the call_id in a chained request, which gives the model real data for the final answer.
- ✗ **C. Automatic callback:** a function tool definition is only a name, description and parameter schema; it has no URL and the service never calls it.
- ✗ **D. Arguments in instructions:** the arguments are the query, not the answer; without the function result the model can only guess the status.

## Key idea
For Responses function calling, run the function yourself and return a `function_call_output` with the matching `call_id`, chained with `previous_response_id`.
Q007212:
## Function calls are model output, not trusted input
The model only proposes calls; your app executes them. That makes the app responsible for what actually happens. Learn's function calling article lists practices for using functions safely:
- **Validate function calls**: "Always verify the function calls generated by the model. This includes checking the parameters, the function being called, and ensuring that the call aligns with the intended action."
- **Principle of least privilege**: "Grant only the minimum access necessary for the function to perform its job. ... if you're using function calls to query a database, you should only give your application read-only access to the database. You also shouldn't depend solely on excluding capabilities in the function definition as a security control."
## Applying it here
- The balance function uses read-only credentials.
- The transfer function checks that both accounts belong to the signed-in customer and that the amount is within limits before it runs; high-risk actions can also ask the user to confirm.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Validate calls (correct):** checking the function, its arguments and whether the action matches the user's intent stops a wrong or manipulated call before it moves money.
- ✗ **B. Administrator identity:** broad permissions are the opposite of least privilege and turn any bad call into a high-impact one.
- ✗ **C. Raw SQL argument:** letting the model write arbitrary queries widens what a manipulated prompt could do and removes the narrow, checkable parameters.
- ✗ **D. Descriptions as security:** Learn warns against depending only on what the function definition leaves out; descriptions guide the model but enforce nothing.
- ✓ **E. Read-only for queries (correct):** a read-only database identity limits the damage if the balance function is ever misused, exactly as Learn's least-privilege example describes.

## Key idea
Treat model-generated function calls as untrusted: validate them in code and give each function only the access it needs.
Q007213:
## Classic RAG
Azure AI Search's RAG overview describes the **classic RAG pattern**: "your application sends a single query to Azure AI Search and orchestrates the handoff to an LLM separately. Your deployed LLM formulates an answer using the flattened result set from the query." It uses GA features and suits simpler requirements. (Agentic retrieval with knowledge bases is the newer option; its LLM query planning is in preview.)
## Getting the right chunks
For query understanding, Learn lists:
- **Hybrid queries** that combine keyword and vector search for better recall.
- **Semantic ranking** that re-scores results by meaning, not just keywords.
- **Vector similarity** that matches concepts, not exact terms, so "telecommute" can find "remote work".
For token limits it adds configurable result limits (top-k for vectors) and a `select` list that returns only the fields you need.
## Prompt assembly
1. Embed the question and run the hybrid query with semantic ranking.
2. Take the top chunks and format each with an id or title and its content.
3. Send a system message that says to answer only from the sources and cite them, plus the user question and the sources.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. All documents in the system message:** the corpus won't fit the token budget, and Learn's guidance is to return concise, highly relevant results instead.
- ✗ **B. Model first:** answering from training data ignores the company's policies and invites fabricated answers, which RAG exists to prevent.
- ✗ **C. Keyword-only with full documents:** exact-word matching misses "remote work" for "telecommute", and whole documents waste tokens compared with chunks.
- ✓ **D. Hybrid plus semantic ranking, then grounded prompt (correct):** vector and semantic matching bridge the vocabulary gap, and passing only the top chunks with ids keeps the prompt small and citable.

## Key idea
In classic RAG, run a hybrid query with semantic ranking and give the model only the top chunks with source ids and an answer-only-from-sources instruction.
Q007214:
## Citations are something you build
In classic RAG your application assembles the prompt, so the model can only cite what you show it, in the form you show it.
## Step 1: make sources citable
Format each retrieved chunk with an identifier, for example:
`[doc-17] Travel Policy v4: Employees must book economy class for flights under six hours...`
Then instruct the model: answer only from the sources, cite the id in brackets after each claim, and say you don't know if the sources don't cover the question.
## Step 2: verify what came back
Models can still produce a wrong or invented id. Microsoft's On Your Data migration checklist includes "Resolve citations and verify source support" and "Read the answer and validate citation IDs". The app keeps the list of ids it retrieved for the request and drops or flags any citation not in that list before rendering links.
## Why not rely on the model
The model has no knowledge of your private documents beyond the prompt, so "remembered" sources are fabrications.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Automatic citations from search:** in classic RAG the search returns results and the app builds the prompt; nothing attaches citations to the model output for you.
- ✗ **B. Model's own knowledge:** the policies are private, so any source the model "remembers" is a guess rather than a citation.
- ✓ **C. Validate cited ids (correct):** checking citations against the retrieved set catches invented or mismatched ids before an auditor sees them.
- ✗ **D. Higher temperature:** more randomness makes citations less reliable, not more complete.
- ✓ **E. Label chunks and require ids (correct):** giving each chunk an id and requiring per-claim citations is what lets the answer point to a specific document.

## Key idea
For trustworthy RAG citations, label each chunk with an id, require the model to cite ids, and validate cited ids against what was retrieved.
Q007215:
## Azure OpenAI On Your Data has retired
Azure OpenAI On Your Data let a chat completions request carry a `data_sources` configuration so the service queried a source such as Azure AI Search and grounded the answer. Learn now states: "Azure OpenAI On Your Data retired on October 14, 2026, and is no longer supported by Microsoft." The article is kept only for history and migration.
## What still works
"Ordinary Azure OpenAI chat completions requests without On Your Data configuration aren't the retired feature." That's why plain chat calls keep working.
## Migration options
- Call a **Foundry IQ knowledge base** directly for corpus Q&A (Microsoft's migration sample reuses the existing Azure AI Search index). Generally available knowledge base retrieval uses the 2026-04-01 API with app-managed answer generation; the sample's answer synthesis uses a preview API.
- Use **classic RAG**: query Azure AI Search in your app and generate the answer yourself.
- Add Foundry Agent Service when you also need tools or workflows.
Learn warns: "Removing the On Your Data configuration alone doesn't replace retrieval or preserve document-level authorization." Migration isn't automatic.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Recreate the index:** the index is fine; existing indexes can be reused in the migration. The request fails because the feature that read them is gone.
- ✓ **B. Migrate off On Your Data (correct):** the feature behind the `data_sources` block is retired, so the app needs a supported retrieval path such as a Foundry IQ knowledge base or its own classic RAG code.
- ✗ **C. Just remove data_sources:** without the block, nothing retrieves documents; the model would answer from training data and lose any per-user authorization.
- ✗ **D. Older api-version:** retirement applies to the feature, not to one API version, so no version string brings it back.

## Key idea
Azure OpenAI On Your Data retired on 2026-10-14; replace `data_sources` requests with a Foundry IQ knowledge base or app-managed RAG.
Q007216:
## Finding affected applications
Microsoft's retirement guidance has a section titled "Identify affected applications": "Search your application requests, code, and configuration for `data_sources`, the legacy `dataSources`, and the `/extensions/chat/completions` path. These are signals that an application uses Azure OpenAI On Your Data."
## What isn't affected
- Ordinary chat completions or Responses calls without an On Your Data configuration.
- Apps that already do **classic RAG** themselves: they call Azure AI Search and put the results in the prompt. That's the supported pattern the migration points to.
- The authentication method or the endpoint format; these don't indicate On Your Data.
## Example audit
A simple repository search for `data_sources`, `dataSources` and `extensions/chat/completions` across code and gateway logs produces the list of apps to migrate.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bearer token auth:** keyless authentication is unrelated to whether a request uses On Your Data.
- ✓ **B. /extensions/chat/completions path (correct):** the older On Your Data requests used this extensions path, so its presence marks an affected app.
- ✗ **C. App-side search:** querying Azure AI Search in code and passing results to the model is classic RAG, which is the supported replacement.
- ✗ **D. v1 endpoint and deployment name:** that's the standard way to call any deployment and says nothing about On Your Data.
- ✓ **E. data_sources property (correct):** this request property (and its older camel-case form) is how an app hands retrieval configuration to On Your Data.

## Key idea
Apps that use On Your Data show `data_sources`/`dataSources` in request bodies or call `/extensions/chat/completions`.
Q007217:
## Fabrication in RAG
A RAG response can be well written and on topic yet still include claims the sources don't support. That's a **fabrication** (also called an ungrounded claim or hallucination) and it's a precision problem: the answer contains something it shouldn't.
## Matching evaluators to failures
From Learn's RAG and general-purpose evaluator articles:
- **Groundedness**: "how well the generated response aligns with the given context without fabricating content (precision aspect)". Inputs: response and context (query optional, recommended).
- **Relevance**: whether the response accurately addresses the query (query, response).
- **Response Completeness** (preview): the recall side, whether the response misses information in the ground truth.
- **Coherence** and **Fluency**: writing quality, "independent of factual correctness".
AI-assisted evaluators like these score 1 to 5 with a default pass threshold of 3.
## Example
Context: "Items can be returned within 30 days with receipt." Response: "Returns are accepted within 30 days, and shipping is refunded." The refund claim isn't in the context, so groundedness drops even though relevance stays high.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Relevance:** the answers are on topic, so relevance stays high; it doesn't check claims against the context.
- ✗ **B. Fluency:** fluency judges language quality, and Learn notes these writing-quality evaluators are independent of factual correctness.
- ✗ **C. Coherence:** a fabricated claim can be perfectly logical and well connected; coherence measures flow, not support.
- ✓ **D. Groundedness (correct):** it compares the response with the retrieved context and penalizes content the context doesn't support, which is exactly the added return-policy details.

## Key idea
To catch fabricated content in RAG answers, run the Groundedness evaluator with the response and the retrieved context.
Q007218:
## Evaluators need specific fields
Every built-in evaluator reads named fields from the test data through a data mapping such as `{{item.query}}`. If a required field is missing, that evaluator can't score the row. Learn's tables list the required inputs:
- **Relevance**: query, response
- **Coherence**: query, response (or messages)
- **Fluency**: response (or messages)
- **Groundedness**: response plus the grounding context (query optional)
- **Retrieval**: query, context
- **Similarity**: query, response, ground_truth
- **F1, BLEU, ROUGE and similar NLP metrics**: ground_truth, response
AI-assisted evaluators (Relevance, Coherence, Fluency, Groundedness, Retrieval, Similarity) also need a judge model `deployment_name`.
## Planning test data
Decide which metrics you need before you collect data. If groundedness matters, log the retrieved context with each response; if you want similarity or F1, write expected answers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. F1 score:** it compares the response with a ground truth answer word by word, and the file has no expected answers.
- ✗ **B. Retrieval:** it scores the retrieved context against the query, and there's no context to score.
- ✓ **C. Fluency (correct):** it scores the response text alone, so the file is enough.
- ✗ **D. Similarity:** it compares the response with a ground truth answer, which the file lacks.
- ✓ **E. Relevance (correct):** it needs only the query and the response, which every line has.

## Key idea
Match evaluators to the data you have: query plus response supports Relevance, Coherence and Fluency; Retrieval needs context; Similarity and F1 need ground truth.
Q007219:
## Two families of ground-truth metrics
Learn's textual similarity article separates them:
- **Similarity** (`builtin.similarity`): an LLM judge "focuses on semantics of a response, instead of simple overlap in tokens or n-grams. It also considers the broader context of a query." Inputs: query, response, ground_truth; a judge `deployment_name`; 1-5 score, default threshold 3.
- **F1, BLEU, GLEU, ROUGE, METEOR**: algorithmic overlap of tokens or n-grams; no judge model; 0-1 float, default threshold 0.5. METEOR adds some synonym and stemming handling.
## Choosing
Learn: "Use `builtin.similarity` when semantic meaning matters — for example, when paraphrases or synonyms should score as equivalent. Use the algorithmic evaluators ... when exact token overlap is the criterion, such as machine translation quality assessment, fixed-answer retrieval, or NLP benchmarking." All six are GA.
## Example
"Paris is France's largest city" vs "The largest city in France is Paris": overlap metrics are reduced by the reordering and word changes, while Similarity rates them as equivalent.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Similarity (correct):** an LLM judge compares meaning with the teacher's answer, so a correct paraphrase scores well even when the wording differs.
- ✗ **B. F1 score:** it counts shared words, so paraphrases with different vocabulary lose points even when they are correct.
- ✗ **C. ROUGE:** it measures n-gram overlap with a recall focus; reworded answers still score lower than their correctness deserves.
- ✗ **D. BLEU:** it rewards exact n-gram matches, which suits translation benchmarks rather than free-form correct answers.

## Key idea
Use the Similarity evaluator when paraphrases should count as correct; F1, BLEU and ROUGE reward exact word overlap.
Q007220:
## Process versus system evaluation in RAG
Learn splits RAG evaluators into:
- **System evaluation** of the final response: Groundedness, Relevance, Response Completeness (preview).
- **Process evaluation** of the retrieval step: **Retrieval** and **Document Retrieval**.
## Document Retrieval
Use it when "retrieval quality is a bottleneck for your RAG, and you have query relevance labels (ground truth)". It compares `retrieved_documents` (ids with search scores) with `retrieval_ground_truth` (ids with human `query_relevance_label` values) and returns:
- **Fidelity**: how many of the known good documents were returned
- **NDCG** and **XDCG**: ranking quality in the top results
- **Max relevance N**: best relevance in the top-k
- **Holes**: retrieved documents with no relevance label
It needs no judge model.
## Parameter sweep
Learn describes generating retrieval results for different search settings (search algorithms, top_k, chunk sizes) and using `document_retrieval` "to find the search parameters that yield the highest retrieval quality".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Document Retrieval (correct):** with human labels it computes standard search metrics such as NDCG and fidelity, which is what a parameter sweep across search settings needs.
- ✗ **B. Groundedness:** it evaluates the final answer against context, so it can't tell which search setting ranked documents better.
- ✗ **C. Relevance:** it scores the generated answer against the query; poor ranking and poor generation look the same in this score.
- ✗ **D. Retrieval:** it's the choice when you don't have labels; it returns an LLM-judged 1-5 score, not NDCG or fidelity.

## Key idea
With human relevance labels, use the Document Retrieval evaluator (NDCG, XDCG, fidelity, holes) to compare search settings for RAG.
Q007221:
## Evaluation targets in the Foundry portal
When you create an evaluation, you first choose what it runs against. Learn's portal evaluation article lists:
- **Agent**: runs your agent on the inputs and scores its outputs.
- **Model**: runs a deployed model on your prompts and scores what it generates.
- **Dataset**: "Evaluates preexisting model or agent outputs from a test dataset." Learn's summary: "Evaluating preexisting outputs without re-running the model or agent."
- **Traces**: scores agent interactions already captured in Application Insights.
## Data sources
A dataset is a CSV or JSONL file. Other options include existing datasets for model benchmarking and synthetic data, where AI generates test queries.
## Choosing
If you want to know how *last month's answers* scored, re-running the model would score different answers from a possibly different model version. A dataset target scores the logged answers exactly as users saw them. Map the file's columns (for example `query`, `response`) to the evaluators' inputs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Synthetic data:** generated questions replace the real ones, losing the production set the team wants to measure.
- ✓ **B. Dataset target (correct):** it scores the answers already in the file, so the results describe exactly what users received and no inference is repeated.
- ✗ **C. Agent with simulated data:** simulation creates new synthetic conversations; it doesn't score recorded answers.
- ✗ **D. Model target:** it generates fresh answers, which may differ from the logged ones and wouldn't measure last month's quality.

## Key idea
To score outputs you already have, use a Dataset evaluation target; Model and Agent targets generate new outputs first.
Q007222:
## Two kinds of built-in evaluators
- **AI-assisted (LLM-as-judge)**: Coherence, Fluency, Relevance, Groundedness, Retrieval, Similarity. A judge model reads the inputs and scores them on a 1-5 scale. Learn lists `deployment_name` as a **required parameter**; general-purpose evaluator guidance suggests gpt-5-mini as a good balance of performance and cost.
- **Algorithmic**: F1, BLEU, GLEU, ROUGE, METEOR. They compute token or n-gram overlap and need no judge model; F1, BLEU, GLEU and METEOR list no required parameters (ROUGE only needs a `rouge_type`).
## Cloud evaluation setup
The cloud evaluation article sets shared variables: `AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT` and `AZURE_AI_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME` ("the model deployment used by AI-assisted evaluators"), then creates `AIProjectClient` and its OpenAI client. A criterion for an AI-assisted evaluator looks like:
`{"type": "azure_ai_evaluator", "name": "coherence", "evaluator_name": "builtin.coherence", "initialization_parameters": {"deployment_name": model_deployment}, "data_mapping": {"query": "{{item.query}}", "response": "{{item.response}}"}}`
## Why F1 still worked
F1 only needs `ground_truth` and `response`, so it ran without a judge.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Threshold:** thresholds decide pass or fail after scoring; they don't prevent an evaluator from starting.
- ✗ **B. ground_truth column:** coherence needs query and response (or messages); ground truth is for Similarity and the NLP metrics.
- ✗ **C. Application Insights:** connecting it lets results flow to monitoring, but it isn't required for an evaluator to run.
- ✓ **D. Judge deployment name (correct):** coherence is scored by an LLM judge, and without `deployment_name` in its initialization parameters the evaluator has no model to call.

## Key idea
AI-assisted evaluators need a judge model `deployment_name`; algorithmic metrics such as F1 and BLEU don't.
Q007223:
## What a connection is
Learn: "Connections let you authenticate to Microsoft and other resources within your Foundry projects." Azure AI Search, Azure Storage, Application Insights, Azure Key Vault and other services can be connected. Connection details are stored in a managed Key Vault unless you bring your own.
## Reading connections from code
The Azure AI Projects client library (part of the Foundry SDK) lets you "enumerate connected Azure resources in your Foundry project using `.connections` operations", alongside `.deployments`, `.datasets` and `.indexes`. Learn's SDK overview places "listing connections" among the project client's Foundry-native operations.
## Example flow
1. Configure only `FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT` per environment.
2. `project = AIProjectClient(endpoint=..., credential=DefaultAzureCredential())`
3. Use `project.connections` to find the Azure AI Search connection and read its target endpoint.
4. Create the `SearchClient` with that endpoint and a keyless credential.
Each environment's project points to its own search service, so the code stays the same.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. models.list on v1:** that lists models available to the resource; search services aren't models and aren't returned.
- ✗ **B. Resource Manager query:** picking the first search service in a subscription is fragile and ignores which service the project actually uses.
- ✓ **C. Project connections (correct):** the project client's connections operations expose the connected search resource, so the app needs only the project endpoint per environment.
- ✗ **D. Deployments list:** deployments describe models (name, version, capacity, guardrails), not search indexes.

## Key idea
Let apps discover connected resources such as Azure AI Search through `AIProjectClient` connections operations, configured with just the project endpoint.
Q007224:
## The v1 Azure OpenAI API
Since August 2025, you can opt in to the **v1** API. Learn lists what it changes:
- "`OpenAI()` client is used instead of `AzureOpenAI()`."
- "Pass the Azure OpenAI endpoint to `base_url` and append `/openai/v1` to the endpoint address."
- "`api-version` is no longer a required parameter with the v1 GA API."
Preview features are opted into with feature-specific headers or path segments instead of changing API versions.
## Before and after
Before: `AzureOpenAI(azure_endpoint=..., api_key=..., api_version="2024-xx-xx")`
After: `OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY"), base_url="https://<resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/")`
The request still names the **deployment** in `model`. Keys still work; with Entra ID you pass a token provider as `api_key` instead.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Project endpoint:** the v1 API lives on the resource endpoint `https://<resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/`; the project endpoint is for the Foundry SDK.
- ✗ **B. Catalog model name:** the `model` field still takes the deployment name on the v1 endpoint.
- ✓ **C. /openai/v1/ and no api_version (correct):** the v1 route uses implicit versioning, so the base URL changes and the dated version parameter goes away.
- ✗ **D. Key as connection secret:** the v1 examples pass the API key straight to `OpenAI(api_key=...)`; connections aren't involved.
- ✓ **E. OpenAI() client (correct):** the v1 API is designed for the standard OpenAI client, so `AzureOpenAI()` isn't needed anymore.

## Key idea
Moving to v1 means `OpenAI()` with `base_url=https://<resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/` and no `api_version`, still naming the deployment in `model`.
Q007225:
## Quota versus deployment rate limit
In Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI quota is granted to a subscription **per region, per model and per deployment type**, in tokens per minute (TPM). Quota is a pool, not a limit on traffic by itself:
- When you create a deployment you **assign** part of that pool to it, for example 10,000 TPM.
- The assigned TPM becomes the deployment's **TPM rate limit**, and a matching **requests per minute (RPM)** limit is derived from it.
- Unassigned quota sits idle. It does not raise any deployment's limit until you assign it.
## Reading the 429
Learn separates several kinds of 429. "Requests to ... have been limited" or "Rate limit is exceeded" means traffic exceeded the TPM or RPM of **this deployment's allocation**; the recommended action is to increase the deployment's TPM, rebalance quota across deployments, or request more quota. Learn also warns that you can have approved quota at the subscription level and still hit 429s because the quota is not allocated to the deployment receiving the traffic.
## Example
Quota 200,000 TPM, assigned 10,000 TPM. Editing the deployment (Deployments page or Management > Model quota) to 60,000 TPM raises its limit at once and leaves 140,000 TPM for other deployments.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Quota increase request:** the subscription still has 190,000 TPM unassigned, so the pool is not exhausted; the bottleneck is the allocation of this one deployment.
- ✓ **B. Raise deployment TPM (correct):** the deployment is throttled at its own 10,000 TPM allocation while 190,000 TPM of regional quota is unassigned, so assigning more TPM to it lifts the rate limit with no support request.
- ✗ **C. Raise max_tokens:** the rate limiter counts the prompt plus max_tokens for each request, so a larger max_tokens uses up the TPM budget faster and makes the 429s worse.
- ✗ **D. Convert to provisioned:** TPM on a Standard deployment can be changed after creation in increments of 1,000, and provisioned throughput is a billing and capacity decision, not the fix for an under-allocated deployment.

## Key idea
A 429 "rate limit exceeded" with unassigned quota left means the deployment's own TPM allocation is too small; assign more TPM to that deployment.
Q007226:
## How the TPM limit is counted
The TPM rate limit is **not** applied to the tokens you are billed for. When a request arrives, the service computes an **estimated maximum processed-token count** from:
- the prompt text and its length
- the `max_tokens` setting
- the `best_of` setting
That estimate is added to a running counter that resets every minute. When the counter reaches the deployment's TPM, further requests get **429** until it resets.
## Why the metrics look low
Token usage metrics in Azure Monitor (such as Processed Inference Tokens) show **billed tokens from successfully processed requests**. A request with `max_tokens=4000` reserves about 4,000 completion tokens of rate-limit budget even if the model writes only 150. Learn lists "max_tokens overestimation" as a common reason for 429s while usage metrics sit well below quota.
## Example
A 1,000-token prompt with `max_tokens=4000` counts about 5,000 tokens toward the limit. With `max_tokens=300` it counts about 1,300, so almost four times as many requests fit in the same TPM.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Lower max_tokens (correct):** the limiter reserves prompt plus max_tokens per request, so a 4,000 ceiling for 150-token answers burns the TPM budget long before billed usage gets close; sizing max_tokens to the expected reply fixes the throttling.
- ✗ **B. Pin an older api-version:** the TPM limit belongs to the deployment's allocation, not to the API version used to call it, so changing api-version gives no extra allowance.
- ✗ **C. Disable prompt caching:** caching does not double-count tokens against the limit, and turning it off would not touch the inflated max_tokens reservation that is causing the 429s.
- ✗ **D. Metrics lag, quota increase:** the gap is not a delay; billed-token metrics and the request-time estimate measure different things, so asking for more quota treats the wrong cause.

## Key idea
Rate limits count prompt plus max_tokens when the request arrives, not billed tokens, so oversized max_tokens causes 429s even when usage metrics look low.
Q007227:
## RPM is enforced in short windows
The requests-per-minute (RPM) limit expects traffic to be **evenly spread across the minute**. Azure OpenAI evaluates the incoming rate over a small period, typically **1 or 10 seconds**. If more requests arrive in that window than the RPM implies, new requests get 429 until the next window.
- A 600 RPM deployment checked on 1-second windows throttles once more than 10 requests arrive in one second.
- So a burst at 02:00:00 can be throttled even though the minute's total is under the limit.
## Handling 429 correctly
Learn's guidance:
- Use the `retry-after-ms` header on the 429 when present; otherwise use **exponential backoff with random jitter**.
- Cap the number of retries (for example 5 to 10).
- **Unsuccessful requests still count toward the per-minute rate limit**, so resending without backing off makes throttling worse.
- Avoid sharp spikes, ramp up gradually, and queue non-urgent work to process it at a controlled rate.
The `x-ratelimit-remaining-requests` and `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens` headers on every response let the client slow down before it hits 429.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Split across API keys:** the rate limit belongs to the deployment's assigned TPM and RPM, not to a key, so both keys share the same counters.
- ✗ **B. Raise best_of:** each increment of best_of multiplies the token estimate counted against the rate limit, so it pushes the job toward more 429s, not fewer.
- ✗ **C. Immediate tight retry loop:** failed requests still count toward the rate limit, so instant resends keep the deployment throttled and stretch out the failures.
- ✓ **D. Queue at a steady rate (correct):** spreading 3,000 requests across the minute keeps each 1- or 10-second window under the RPM-derived threshold, which removes the burst that triggers the 429s.
- ✓ **E. Honor retry-after-ms with backoff (correct):** waiting the advised time, or backing off exponentially with jitter and a retry cap, lets throttled requests succeed without adding more load during the throttled window.

## Key idea
RPM limits are enforced over 1- to 10-second windows, so smooth bursts with a queue and retry 429s with retry-after-ms or exponential backoff with jitter.
Q007228:
## Spillover for provisioned deployments
A provisioned deployment reserves a fixed amount of capacity, measured in provisioned throughput units (PTUs). When it is fully used it returns non-200 responses such as **429**. **Spillover** routes those overage requests to a **standard deployment** in the **same Foundry resource**, so bursts are served at standard (pay-per-token) rates instead of failing.
Prerequisites: a provisioned deployment and a pay-as-you-go deployment of the **same model and version** in the same resource.
## Two ways to turn it on
- **For all requests**: set the deployment property `spilloverDeploymentName` to the standard deployment's name, during creation or on an existing provisioned deployment. No client change.
- **Per request**: send the `x-ms-spillover-deployment` header on the requests that may spill. Requests without the header never spill. If both are set, the deployment property wins.
## Seeing it work
Spilled responses carry `x-ms-spillover-from-deployment` and `x-ms-spillover-error` (for example 429). In Azure Monitor, split the Azure OpenAI Requests metric (it has an `IsSpillover` dimension) or by deployment to compare traffic on each deployment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Per-request header:** x-ms-spillover-deployment works, but it has to be added to each request by the client, which breaks the requirement to leave the application code unchanged.
- ✗ **B. Buy a reservation:** Azure reservations are a billing discount on the PTU meter; Learn states they don't guarantee capacity and do not add PTUs to a deployment.
- ✗ **C. Version upgrade policy:** the policy decides when a deployment moves to a new model version, and it has nothing to do with routing excess traffic.
- ✓ **D. Set spilloverDeploymentName (correct):** the deployment-level property enables spillover for every request to the provisioned deployment, so overflow moves to the matching standard deployment with no change to the shopping assistant's code.

## Key idea
To send provisioned overflow to a standard deployment for all requests without code changes, set spilloverDeploymentName on the provisioned deployment.
Q007229:
## Watching a provisioned deployment
A provisioned deployment has a fixed capacity. Azure Monitor collects platform metrics for it automatically, and **Provisioned-managed Utilization V2** (`AzureOpenAIProvisionedManagedUtilizationV2`) is the capacity gauge:
- It is calculated as `(PTUs consumed / PTUs deployed) x 100`.
- When utilization is **100% or more, calls are throttled and 429 is returned**.
- It can be split by ModelDeploymentName, ModelName, ModelVersion and StreamType.
The older Provisioned-managed Utilization metric is deprecated and replaced by the V2 metric.
## Other metrics and what they mean
- **Azure OpenAI Requests**: call counts, splittable by StatusCode and IsSpillover.
- **Time to Response, Time Between Tokens, Time to Last Byte**: Azure OpenAI latency measures.
- **Latency** under Cognitive Services - HTTP Requests: a legacy metric that Learn says produces misleading results for Azure OpenAI.
- **Blocked Volume**: calls rejected by the content filter.
## Example
A metric alert "Provisioned-managed Utilization V2 average > 85% for 5 minutes" warns the team before throttling starts, so they can add PTUs or enable spillover.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Utilization V2 (correct):** it measures how much of the deployed PTU capacity is in use and the service throttles at 100%, so a threshold below 100% gives a warning before 429s begin.
- ✗ **B. Blocked Volume:** it counts calls rejected by the content filter (guardrails), not calls refused for lack of PTU capacity.
- ✗ **C. Processed Prompt Tokens:** it counts input tokens processed, but it is not a percentage of deployed capacity and has no built-in link to the throttling point.
- ✗ **D. Legacy Latency metric:** it is a generic Cognitive Services HTTP metric that Learn says is not designed for Azure OpenAI and is misleading for diagnosing it; it does not measure PTU capacity.

## Key idea
Alert on Provisioned-managed Utilization V2 to catch a PTU deployment approaching 100% utilization, the point where calls are throttled with 429.
Q007230:
## Per-consumer token limits at the gateway
A deployment's TPM limit applies to **everyone** who calls it. To give each consumer its own limits, put Azure API Management in front of the model and use the **`llm-token-limit`** policy. It limits language model token use **per key**:
- `counter-key`: what to count against, for example the API Management subscription ID of each team.
- `tokens-per-minute`: a rate limit. When it is exceeded the caller gets **429 Too Many Requests** with a `Retry-After` header.
- `token-quota` with `token-quota-period` (Hourly, Daily, Weekly, Monthly or Yearly): a quota. When it is exceeded the caller gets **403 Forbidden**.
- Either the rate, the quota or both must be set, and `estimate-prompt-tokens` (true or false) is a required attribute.
## Example
```
<llm-token-limit counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)"
tokens-per-minute="20000" token-quota="5000000" token-quota-period="Monthly"
estimate-prompt-tokens="false" />
```
Each team's subscription key gets its own 20,000-token-per-minute cap and a 5,000,000-token monthly quota.
## Budgets are alerts
Cost Management budgets track spending and send alerts; they do not block API calls.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. rate-limit-by-key:** this policy counts calls, not tokens; one call can use 50 tokens or 50,000, so it cannot enforce a token budget.
- ✓ **B. llm-token-limit per team (correct):** one policy enforces both a tokens-per-minute cap and a monthly token quota for each counter key, so each team's subscription gets its own limits on the shared deployment.
- ✗ **C. Split deployments by TPM:** a deployment's TPM is a per-minute rate limit only; it has no monthly budget, and splitting the model into three deployments is not needed to separate consumers.
- ✗ **D. Cost Management budgets:** budgets watch spending and notify people when thresholds are crossed, but they do not reject or throttle API calls.

## Key idea
Use API Management's llm-token-limit policy with a per-consumer counter key to enforce both per-minute token caps (429) and token quotas over a period (403).
Q007231:
## How fine-tuned models are billed
Learn lists three charges for Azure OpenAI fine-tuned models:
- **Training**: per token or per hour, depending on the model, while the training job runs.
- **Hosting**: an **hourly cost per deployed model, even if the model is unused**.
- **Inference**: per token, when the model is called.
Learn warns that fine-tuned deployments incur hosting charges while deployed, even in low-usage periods, and advises removing deployments you do not need.
## Finding the meter
In Microsoft Cost Management, group cost analysis by **Resource** and then by **Meter**. Each charge maps to a meter, so a steady hourly hosting meter stands out from token meters, which follow traffic.
## Contrast with base models
A Standard deployment of a base model is billed per token, so with no traffic it has no usage charge. The fine-tuned deployment is the one that keeps costing money while idle.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Base model hourly billing:** Standard deployments are billed per token, so an idle base deployment has no hourly charge, and Batch is a cheaper per-token option for asynchronous jobs.
- ✗ **B. Training data file:** training is charged while the training job runs; an uploaded data file does not create a recurring hourly training charge.
- ✓ **C. Delete the idle fine-tuned deployment (correct):** hosting is billed hourly for as long as the fine-tuned model is deployed, regardless of traffic, so removing it stops the charge and the model can be redeployed later.
- ✗ **D. Reserved capacity estimate:** reservations apply to provisioned throughput, which this team does not use, and a real hosting meter will keep charging every cycle until the deployment is removed.

## Key idea
A deployed fine-tuned model is billed hourly for hosting even with no traffic, so delete fine-tuned deployments you are not using.
Q007232:
## Safety metrics in Azure Monitor
Azure OpenAI publishes a **ContentSafety - Risks&Safety** metric category. These platform metrics are collected automatically, can be split by dimensions and can drive alerts:
- **Blocked Volume** (`RAIRejectedRequests`): calls **rejected** by the content filter. Dimensions include ModelDeploymentName, ModelName, TextType and Category.
- **Harmful Volume Detected** (`RAIHarmfulRequests`): calls detected as harmful in **both block and annotate mode**.
- **Total Volume Sent For Safety Check** (`RAITotalRequests`): all calls evaluated by the content filter.
- **Safety System Event** (`RAISystemEvent`): system events for risks and safety monitoring.
## Picking the right one
"Detected" is broader than "blocked". If a guardrail is set to annotate only, harmful content is flagged and counted in Harmful Volume Detected but the call still succeeds. Blocked Volume counts only the calls that were actually rejected.
## Example
Metric alert: Blocked Volume, total, split by ModelDeploymentName = `triage-chat`, dynamic threshold. Splitting by Category also shows which harm category is driving the blocks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Harmful Volume Detected:** it counts calls detected as harmful in both block and annotate mode, so annotated-only requests would be included, which the team wants to exclude.
- ✓ **B. Blocked Volume (correct):** it counts exactly the calls rejected by the content filter and can be split per deployment, which matches "rejected, not annotated" for one deployment.
- ✗ **C. Requests by StatusCode:** a filtered prompt is reported as a client error mixed with every other bad request, and it is not a server error, so the status code split cannot isolate guardrail rejections.
- ✗ **D. Total Volume Sent For Safety Check:** it counts every call evaluated by the content filter, blocked or not, so it measures traffic volume rather than rejections.

## Key idea
Use Blocked Volume to monitor requests rejected by guardrails; Harmful Volume Detected also counts annotate-only detections.
Q007233:
## Behavior drift from model version upgrades
A Foundry model deployment has two separate versions:
- the **model version** (for example `2024-08-06`), which is the model weights that answer requests
- the **API version** (`api-version`), which is the contract your code uses
A new model version can change output style, format and quality even when nothing in your app changed. That is a form of drift you should monitor for and control.
## Upgrade policies (Standard deployments)
Set per deployment, at deploy time or later in the deployment settings:
- **Upgrade once new default version becomes available**: moves automatically when a new default version is published. This is what surprised the team.
- **Once the current version expires**: stays on the current version and moves automatically only when that version is retired.
- **Opt out of automatic model version upgrades**: you upgrade manually; when the version is retired, the deployment stops working.
With either of the last two, the team decides when to move before the retirement date. Azure notifies customers at least two weeks before a new version becomes the default, and Learn advises testing applications with the new version after release.
## Example
Set `claims-prod` to Once the current version expires, create `claims-next` with the new version, run your evaluation set against both, then upgrade production (or switch the app's deployment name) when the results are acceptable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Stop following the default and test separately (correct):** a policy that no longer moves with each new default version keeps production on the tested version, and a side-by-side deployment lets the team compare the new version before choosing when to switch, ahead of the retirement date.
- ✗ **B. Pin an older api-version:** the API version is the request contract, not the model weights, so pinning it does not undo a model version upgrade.
- ✗ **C. System message:** a system message shapes the prompt the model sees, but it cannot select or hold a model version, so the next default version would still replace the weights the team tested.
- ✗ **D. Provisioned deployment:** there is no weekend-only upgrade behavior, and moving to provisioned throughput changes billing and capacity rather than solving version control.

## Key idea
To stop unexpected behavior drift from model upgrades, take the deployment off "upgrade once new default version becomes available" and test new versions in a separate deployment.
Q007234:
## Where Foundry monitoring data lives
Microsoft Foundry's production monitoring is **integrated with Azure Monitor Application Insights**. Agent telemetry (traces, token counts, latency, run outcomes and evaluation results) is stored in the Application Insights resource **connected to the Foundry project**, and the portal views query it.
The agent **Monitor** tab (the Agent Monitoring Dashboard, currently in preview) shows summary cards and charts for:
- token usage
- latency
- run success rate
- evaluation and red-teaming results, when configured
Its prerequisites are a Foundry project with an agent and **an Application Insights resource connected to the project**. Retention and billing follow the Application Insights settings.
## Access to the data
Viewers also need Azure RBAC access to the Application Insights resource, and Log Analytics Reader on the linked workspace for log-based views.
## Example
No Application Insights connection means nothing to query, so the dashboard is empty even with heavy traffic. After connecting one (and instrumenting tracing), new runs start appearing in the charts.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Foundry Agent Consumer:** this role grants least-privilege access to call agent endpoints; it has no effect on whether runs are recorded for monitoring.
- ✗ **B. Diagnostic setting to storage:** diagnostic settings route platform logs and metrics, but the agent dashboard does not read from a storage account; it queries Application Insights.
- ✓ **C. Connect Application Insights (correct):** the dashboard reads agent telemetry from the project's connected Application Insights resource, so without that connection there is no data to show.
- ✗ **D. Cognitive Services Usages Reader:** this role lets users see subscription quota and usage for deployment checks, and it has nothing to do with agent telemetry.

## Key idea
Foundry's monitoring dashboards read from Application Insights, so connect an Application Insights resource to the project before expecting any agent metrics.
Q007235:
## What indexer status really means
Azure AI Search reports each indexer run with a status:
- **Success**: the run completed. Learn notes that **a run can be successful even if individual documents have errors**, as long as the number of errors is less than the indexer's **Max failed items** setting.
- **Failed**: errors exceeded Max failed items and indexing stopped.
- **In Progress** and **Reset** describe active and fully re-run indexers.
## Where to see per-document problems
- **Azure portal**: select the indexer to see the execution history (up to 50 recent runs). Each run lists start and end times plus **Errors and Warnings**; you can download them as CSV.
- **REST**: `GET https://[service].search.windows.net/indexers/[name]/status?api-version=...` returns `lastResult` and `executionHistory`, with `itemsProcessed`, `itemsFailed` and the error list.
- **Azure Monitor metrics**: Document processed count and Skill execution invocation count, split by indexer, show trends and support alerts.
Warnings are common (for example, PDFs with no extractable text) and don't always mean a problem.
## Example
`itemsProcessed: 10000, itemsFailed: 60` with errors such as "document is too large" points to the 60 missing files to fix and re-index.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Scoring profile hides documents:** scoring profiles change ranking order, they never remove documents from the index count, and Success does not prove every document was indexed.
- ✗ **B. Activity log only:** the activity log records control-plane events such as key retrieval; per-document indexer errors appear in the indexer's execution history and status API.
- ✗ **C. Add a replica:** replicas add query capacity, not storage, and the service reports indexing failures instead of silently dropping documents.
- ✓ **D. Execution details or Get Indexer Status (correct):** a Success run can still contain failed documents below the Max failed items threshold, and the per-run error list names each failed document and why.

## Key idea
An indexer run marked Success can still have failed documents below Max failed items, so check execution history or Get Indexer Status for per-document errors.
Q007236:
## Throttling in Azure AI Search
Azure AI Search throttles when it is at capacity. From the client side:
- a throttled call returns **HTTP 503**
- during indexing, **HTTP 207** can also mean some items failed to index under load
The **Throttled search queries percentage** metric shows the share of queries dropped instead of processed in each minute, and you can alert on it. Resource logs routed to Log Analytics let you chart 503s by operation (`Query.Search`, `Query.Suggest` and so on) over time.
## Replicas versus partitions
- **Replicas** are copies of the index that serve queries; more replicas mean more queries per second and high availability.
- **Partitions** split the index storage and indexing work.
Learn's rule of thumb: a simple fix for most throttling is more resources, **typically replicas for query-based throttling, or partitions for indexing-based throttling**. Both add cost, so first confirm the pattern with metrics.
## Example
Throttling at 10:00 to 12:00 on weekdays, no indexing at those times, rising SearchQueriesPerSecond: add a replica (or two) and watch the throttled percentage drop.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Add replicas (correct):** the 503s come from query load at peak, not indexing, and replicas are the unit that adds query capacity, which is Learn's standard fix for query-based throttling.
- ✗ **B. Raise model TPM:** the model's rate limit and the search service's capacity are separate; a 429 from the model does not cause Azure AI Search to return 503.
- ✗ **C. Add partitions:** partitions mainly add storage and indexing throughput, which Learn ties to indexing-based throttling; indexing here runs only at night, so the daytime query load is not what partitions address.
- ✗ **D. Back to API keys:** the authentication method is not what drives capacity throttling, and returning to keys would weaken security without adding capacity.

## Key idea
HTTP 503 with a rising Throttled search queries percentage during query peaks means the search service needs more replicas; use partitions for indexing load.
Q007237:
## Keyless authentication in Foundry
Foundry accepts two kinds of credentials:
- **API keys**: static secrets that give full access to the resource with no per-user identity, scope or audit.
- **Microsoft Entra ID tokens** (keyless): OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens for the scope `https://ai.azure.com/.default`, checked against Azure RBAC.
Microsoft recommends Entra ID for production. Some features, such as Foundry Agent Service and evaluations, accept only Entra ID.
## Managed identity removes the secret
A **managed identity** is an Entra identity that Azure creates for a resource and whose credentials Azure rotates, so there is nothing to store. In code, `DefaultAzureCredential` uses your `az login` session locally and the managed identity in Azure, so the same code works in both places. The identity needs a data-plane role: for Foundry projects that is **Foundry User**. Learn tells you not to use roles that start with "Cognitive Services" for Foundry work (except Cognitive Services Usages Reader for quota visibility).
## Turning keys off
Keyless code alone leaves the keys valid. Set `disableLocalAuth` to `true` (Bicep/ARM, or `Set-AzCognitiveServicesAccount -DisableLocalAuth $true`), or assign the built-in Azure Policy "Azure AI Services resources should have key access disabled". The change can take minutes to hours to reach the gateway; confirm that an old key now gets HTTP 401.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cognitive Services Contributor:** Learn says not to use Cognitive Services roles for Foundry scenarios; Foundry User is the least-privilege role for building and calling in a project.
- ✗ **B. Daily key rotation:** rotation shortens how long a leaked key is useful, but the app still stores a secret and Entra ID does not treat keys as token-based authentication.
- ✓ **C. Managed identity with Foundry User (correct):** the app gets Entra tokens from its managed identity, so no key is stored, and Foundry User grants the data-plane actions the calls need.
- ✗ **D. Key Vault reference:** the vault protects where the key is stored, but the app still authenticates with the same key, which still must be rotated and still works if leaked.
- ✓ **E. Disable local authentication (correct):** with key access disabled, every API key, including a leaked one, is rejected and only Entra ID tokens are accepted.

## Key idea
Go keyless by giving the app a managed identity with the Foundry User role and DefaultAzureCredential, then disable local (key) authentication on the resource.
Q007238:
## How private endpoint DNS works
When you create a private endpoint for a Foundry resource, Azure changes the public DNS record into a **CNAME to a `privatelink` subdomain** and, by default, creates a **private DNS zone** for that subdomain with an A record pointing at the private endpoint's IP. The zone is linked to the virtual network.
- From **inside the linked virtual network**, the name resolves to the private IP.
- From **outside**, it resolves to the public endpoint, which is blocked when public network access is Disabled.
Clients use **the same connection string** in both cases; no special URL is needed.
## Custom and on-premises DNS
On-premises DNS servers cannot see the Azure private DNS zone. Learn says to configure your DNS server to resolve the Foundry name in the `privatelink` subdomain to the private endpoint IP: delegate or conditionally forward that subdomain to a resolver that can query the private DNS zone (for example Azure DNS Private Resolver in the hub), or add the A records to your DNS server yourself.
## Example
`contoso-ai.services.ai.azure.com` -> CNAME `contoso-ai.privatelink.services.ai.azure.com`. On-premises DNS forwards `privatelink.services.ai.azure.com` to the hub resolver and gets `10.20.1.5`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Re-enable public access:** private endpoint DNS does not depend on the public endpoint, and opening public access defeats the network isolation requirement.
- ✗ **B. Foundry User role:** a public IP in nslookup is a name resolution problem; RBAC applies only after a request reaches the service and would not change DNS answers.
- ✗ **C. New privatelink hostname:** Learn states that clients behind the private endpoint use the same connection string as public clients; DNS, not the URL, decides which address is reached.
- ✓ **D. Fix on-premises name resolution (correct):** the endpoint is reached only through the private IP, and the on-premises DNS returns the public address, so forwarding the privatelink zone to Azure or adding the A record makes the same hostname resolve privately.

## Key idea
When on-premises clients resolve a private-endpoint Foundry resource to its public IP, make on-premises DNS resolve the privatelink name to the private endpoint IP.
Q007239:
## Indexer connections without secrets
An indexer reads source content through a **data source** object. A classic Blob Storage connection string carries an account key or a SAS token, which is a secret. Azure AI Search can instead connect with a **managed identity** (Basic tier or higher):
- Enable a system-assigned (or user-assigned) managed identity on the **search service**.
- In the storage account's Access control (IAM), give that identity the data role for the task: **Storage Blob Data Reader** for blob indexing (Storage Table Data Reader for tables).
- Set the data source connection string to a **ResourceId** with no account key or password. A user-assigned identity also needs the `identity` property on the data source.
The connection and role assignment are validated when the indexer runs.
## Shared Key disabled
With `AllowSharedKeyAccess` set to false, Blob Storage rejects requests authorized with Shared Key. Account SAS and service SAS tokens are signed with the account key, so they are rejected too; Microsoft Entra authorization (and user delegation SAS) still works.
## Firewalled storage
If the storage account is also network-protected and in the same region as the search service, Learn requires the system-assigned identity plus either the trusted service exception or a resource instance rule.
## Example
`"connectionString": "ResourceId=/subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-rag/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stpolicies/;"` with Storage Blob Data Reader assigned to the search service's identity on `stpolicies`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Foundry project identity:** the indexer runs inside the search service and connects as the search service's own managed identity, so a role given to the project's identity is never used.
- ✓ **B. Search service identity with Storage Blob Data Reader (correct):** the indexer authenticates to Blob Storage with the search service's Entra identity, which is unaffected by disabling Shared Key, and the ResourceId connection string contains no secret.
- ✗ **C. Account SAS token:** an account SAS is signed with the storage account key, so it is rejected when Shared Key access is disallowed, and it is still a secret stored in the data source.
- ✗ **D. Search Index Data Reader:** it is a search data-plane role that authorizes queries on search indexes; it grants no blob read actions on a storage account.

## Key idea
To index Blob Storage without secrets, give the search service a managed identity, assign it Storage Blob Data Reader and use a ResourceId connection string.
Q007240:
## Where Foundry stores connection secrets
Connections let a Foundry project reach other services. Connections that use Microsoft Entra ID need no stored secret. For connections that use keys or other secrets:
- **By default**, Foundry stores connection details in a **Microsoft-managed Key Vault outside your subscription**.
- To manage the secrets yourself, add an **Azure Key Vault connection** (bring your own vault).
## Rules for a bring-your-own vault
- The Foundry resource must have **no existing connections** at the resource or project level when you add it.
- **One Azure Key Vault connection per Foundry resource.**
- Foundry **does not migrate secrets**; you remove and recreate connections yourself.
- **Deleting the vault breaks the Foundry resource**: every feature that depends on secret-based connections stops working. Deleting individual secrets can break other connections.
- The Foundry resource's managed identity needs a role on the vault; **Key Vault Secrets Officer** is the minimal role (Key Vault Contributor or Administrator also work).
## Tip
Prefer Entra ID connections wherever the target service supports them, so fewer secrets need a vault at all.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Per-project vaults:** the limit is one Key Vault connection per Foundry resource, and deleting the vault breaks the whole resource, not one project.
- ✓ **B. Before other connections, one per resource (correct):** Learn requires a Foundry resource with no existing connections and allows only one Key Vault connection per Foundry resource, so it must be planned at setup time.
- ✗ **C. Automatic migration:** Foundry does not support secret migration, which is why the connection must exist before other connections are created.
- ✗ **D. Plain text in project storage:** the default store is a Microsoft-managed Key Vault outside your subscription, not plain text, and adding a vault does not re-encrypt or move anything.

## Key idea
Add a bring-your-own Key Vault connection to a Foundry resource before any other connections exist; only one is allowed and secrets are never migrated.
Q007241:
## Data-plane access to Azure AI Search
A new search service accepts **API keys only** for data-plane calls (create, load and query indexes). To use Microsoft Entra ID tokens, including tokens from a managed identity, you must **enable role-based access control**:
- **API keys**: the default; tokens are not accepted.
- **Role-based access control** (recommended): tokens only.
- **Both**: keys or tokens; meant for the transition period. If a request carries both, the key is used.
## Roles
- **Search Index Data Reader**: read-only query access to index content. By default it applies to all indexes; it can be scoped to a single index.
- **Search Index Data Contributor**: load and change index content.
- **Search Service Contributor**: manage the service and its objects (indexes, indexers). Learn warns that Owner, Contributor and Search Service Contributor can retrieve admin keys, which give full read-write access to the data plane.
## Example
Enable RBAC, then assign Search Index Data Reader on the `policies-index` to the backend's managed identity. The backend's token now authorizes queries, and nothing else.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Foundry User:** Foundry roles authorize Foundry resources and projects; Azure AI Search checks its own Search Index Data roles on the search service.
- ✗ **B. Trusted service exception:** this is a Storage firewall feature that lets the search service's own identity reach blobs for indexing; it does not bypass authentication for callers of the search service.
